A docket is an official list or schedule of things that need to be dealt with. Think of it as a formal "to-do list" — but one that belongs to an institution, not a person. It keeps track of matters that are pending, in progress, or recorded for official purposes.

This word is used in a few different but related contexts, and understanding each one will give you a complete picture.

1. A Court's Schedule of Cases (most common modern use)

In a legal setting, a docket is the official list of all cases that a court has to handle. Every lawsuit, criminal case, or legal dispute gets added to the court's docket. It tells the court: which cases exist, when they will be heard, and what stage each case is at.

Think of it like a court's appointment book — except instead of doctor visits, it's filled with legal cases.

When lawyers say a case is "on the docket," they mean it is officially scheduled and registered with the court, waiting for its turn to be heard.

When there are too many cases waiting, lawyers say the court has a "crowded docket" or "backlogged docket" — meaning the court is overwhelmed with work.

2. A Record of What Happened in a Court Case

A docket is also the official written record of everything that has happened in a specific legal case — every filing, every court order, every hearing date, every document submitted. It's essentially a case history log.

If you've ever looked up a court case online, you've seen this kind of docket. It looks like a timeline, listing entries like:

  • "Complaint filed — January 3"
  • "Defendant's response submitted — January 20"
  • "Hearing scheduled — February 10"

Each individual entry on this log is called a docket entry. The number assigned to each entry is called a docket number, which is used to identify and track that specific case across the entire court system.

3. A List of Items for Any Official Meeting or Agenda

Outside of courts, docket can also refer to a list of topics, issues, or tasks lined up for discussion or action at any official setting — a government committee, a legislative body, a formal meeting, etc.

Example: "Three major policy changes are on the docket for this week's council meeting."

Here, it simply means: these are the things officially lined up to be addressed. It's a slightly more formal way of saying "agenda."

4. A Label or Tag Attached to Goods (older and British usage)

In an older and largely British commercial sense, a docket was a physical tag, ticket, or label attached to a package, parcel, or shipment. It contained key details about the contents — what's inside, where it's going, who it's for, or what duties have been paid on it.

Think of it like the label stuck to a box at a shipping warehouse, carrying all the important information about that package.

This meaning is mostly found in historical texts, legal documents from the UK, or customs and trade contexts. In everyday modern speech, especially in American English, this sense is rare.
The Thread That Connects All the Meanings

Notice what all these meanings share: a docket is always about organizing, recording, and tracking — whether it's court cases, legal proceedings, agenda items, or packages. It's never informal or casual. A docket always implies something official, structured, and systematic.
